title: The Company Replacing BLS for Indian Passport Services in the UAE Promises 16 Centres, Lower Fees, and 300 New Jobs
excerpt: Kerala-based Alhind Group takes over consular outsourcing for 4.3 million Indians from July 1 — the biggest operational shift in Gulf passport services in over a decade.
body:
Every Indian in the UAE who has ever queued for a passport renewal, filed an OCI application, or scrambled for an emergency travel document knows the name BLS International. That 15-year relationship ends on July 1, 2026. Kerala-based Alhind Group is taking over, and the scale of the transition is enormous: 16 new service centres across all seven emirates, a flat fee structure, aggressive digitisation, and more than 300 new jobs.

**How the Contract Changed Hands**

The Indian Embassy in Abu Dhabi awarded the outsourcing contract after a competitive tender involving four bidders: Alhind, VFS Global, DU Digital Global, and SGIVS Global. Alhind won on the strength of its financial offer — the lowest bid. The contract covers passport renewals and new applications, Indian visa processing, OCI card services, police clearance certificates, surrender certificates, Global Entry Program verification, and apostille and certification services.

The shift comes two years after the Ministry of External Affairs barred BLS International from participating in new Indian mission tenders, citing complaints and legal cases. For the 4.3 million Indians in the UAE — the country's largest expatriate community — the change is not just administrative. It touches almost every major life event that requires consular paperwork: visa renewals, family sponsorship, newborn registration, and emergency travel.

**What Changes for You**

The most immediately visible difference will be the number of service centres. Alhind plans to operate in 16 locations, including Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Fujairah, Al Ain, Kalba, and Khor Fakkan. For Indian residents outside downtown Dubai and Abu Dhabi, this expansion could significantly reduce travel time for routine appointments.

On pricing, Alhind has committed to a flat all-inclusive service fee of 19 dirhams above the embassy charge, which includes photography and photocopying. "We want to make this process as affordable as possible," said Mohammad Harish T, outlining the company's plans.

The company also intends to digitise back-end operations. "The website will change, the process will be similar, but we plan to digitize everything," said Arun Radhakrishnan, describing upgraded online systems and digital processing tools that Alhind will roll out.

**The Jobs Windfall**

The transition is generating a significant recruitment wave. Alhind has announced more than 300 new positions, including submission officers, operations executives, branch heads, and front-office staff. Fresh graduates holding valid UAE residence visas are also being considered — a rare opportunity for young Indians already in the country.

**The Risks**

Industry observers are watching the July 1 switchover closely. Even small disruptions could impact thousands of appointments, travel plans, and document submissions daily. Concerns have been raised about operational readiness, staffing levels, and data security — consular systems handle sensitive personal documents, biometric details, and financial information.

The first few months will be the acid test. Alhind has experience managing document systems and operates authorised certification centres across India, but running 16 centres serving millions of people in a new country is a different scale of operation entirely.

**The NRI Takeaway**

For the millions of Indians in the Gulf — labourers in Sharjah, engineers in Abu Dhabi, entrepreneurs in Dubai — consular services are not a bureaucratic abstraction. They are the thread that keeps their legal status, family ties, and travel plans intact. A smoother, cheaper, more accessible system would be genuinely transformative. Whether Alhind delivers on that promise starts becoming clear in about six weeks.
